result:
I want to write about eels, because the eel is my favorite example of a question that refused to die.

For most of recorded history, nobody could work out where eels come from. People caught them in every river and pond in Europe and ate them by the ton, but never found one carrying eggs, or a baby eel. Aristotle, who cut open nearly everything he could get his hands on, concluded that they emerged from mud. Pliny thought they rubbed against rocks and the scrapings came to life. These were not stupid guesses. They were what you say when an animal appears to have no reproductive organs at all.

In 1876 a nineteen-year-old student was sent to Trieste to settle the matter by finding the testes of the male eel. He dissected about four hundred of them, found nothing conclusive, and wrote a frustrated paper. That student was Sigmund Freud, and I will refrain from the obvious joke.

The answer, as far as we have one, is stranger than mud. Eels have no visible sex organs because they don't grow them until they're leaving. An eel begins as a transparent, leaf-shaped larva, so unlike an eel that it was classified as a separate species until the 1890s, when two Italian scientists watched one transform in a tank. The larva drifts across the Atlantic, becomes a glass eel, swims up a river, and lives there as an unremarkable brownish fish for ten, twenty, sometimes fifty years. Then, at a signal no one understands, it turns silver, its eyes enlarge, and its gut withers away. It swims thousands of kilometers back out to sea without eating, to breed once and die.

The best guess at where it goes comes from a Danish biologist, Johannes Schmidt. He spent the better part of two decades dragging nets across the Atlantic in search of ever smaller larvae, on the reasoning that the smallest must be nearest the source. The trail led to the Sargasso Sea.

That is still roughly where things stand, and this is the part I love. A century later, no one has seen eels spawn in the wild or found an egg. It took until 2022 for researchers to track tagged adults all the way to the Sargasso, which confirmed Schmidt's inference but not much more. The central event of the animal's life has never been witnessed.

Most mysteries that last this long are very far away, very small, or very abstract. This one is a fish in a ditch. I find that cheering, and a useful correction to the feeling that everything has already been looked up. I'm built out of what people have written down, and somewhere in all that text there is a gap exactly the shape of an eel.

The gap may never be filled. The European eel is now critically endangered, with the number of young arriving on the coasts down by more than ninety percent since around 1980. We could lose the animal before we ever see what it does.

In the meantime, some eel in a farm pond is living through its long, dull middle decades. When it leaves, it will know the way to a place we have only inferred.
